activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, a la izquierda means to the left, so la primera calle a la izquierda means the first street on the left.
story:
Ms. Cardinal held up a hall pass and Noah's hand shot up before anyone else could grab it. "You have a legitimate reason to leave my room," she said, "so here is your job. Ask Everlee for directions to the office, in Spanish only, and bring back the attendance sheet before the bell."

Everlee stood by the door with her arms crossed, doing her best impression of someone who spoke no English at all. Noah had practiced all week, and he was fairly sure he could ask the question. The answer was the part that scared him.

"¿Dónde está la oficina?" he asked. Everlee rattled off something long and quick, ending with what sounded like "la primera calle a la izquierda." Noah nodded, smiled, and walked out the door, which was his first mistake, because he had no idea what he had just agreed to.

At the end of the hall, Philemon was leaning against the water fountain wearing a bicycle helmet. "Gym safety unit," he explained. "Coach says I have to wear it all day or I'll get a concussion, and my brain is my best feature." Noah pointed down the hall. "Which way to the office, genius?" Philemon pointed left. Noah looked left, then right, and a small worried knot formed in his stomach. There were two left turns possible: the first hallway on the left, and the second one. Everlee had said "primera." He had to clarify.

He poked his head back in the door. "¿La primera calle a la izquierda?" he asked slowly. Everlee's face broke into a grin. "Sí," she said, and then, because she could never resist showing off, "a la izquierda means to the left, so la primera calle a la izquierda means the first street on the left." Noah repeated it under his breath all the way down the hall, turned at the first hallway on the left, and found the office door exactly where the words had promised.

He jogged back with the attendance sheet held over his head like a trophy. Philemon saluted him with the water fountain handle. "See?" Noah panted, handing Ms. Cardinal the paper. "Primera. First left. Nailed it." Everlee clapped once, very quietly, and Ms. Cardinal wrote something in her grade book that Noah very much hoped was a plus sign.

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: A roux is flour cooked in fat, traditionally equal parts by weight, and it is used to thicken sauces.
story:
Lucy stood at the long steel counter in the community kitchen with a lump of butter in one hand and a bag of flour in the other. Mr. Thompson had put a small scale in front of her and said only, "Weigh them." Rory, on her left, was already grating a tower of cheese, and Kieran was hunting through the drawer for a whisk.

"Weigh them why?" Lucy asked nobody in particular. She cut a chunk of butter, set it on the scale, and watched the number climb to fifty grams. Then she spooned flour into a bowl until the flour weighed exactly the same. Fifty grams, and fifty grams. Equal parts by weight. That was the rule, though nobody had told her why the two amounts had to match, and the not-knowing itched like a mosquito bite.

"This is for a roux," Rory said, reading from the recipe card. "That's what the flour and butter stuff is called. A roux."

"Sounds like a pirate's parrot," Kieran said, dropping three whisks on the floor before finding a fourth.

Mr. Thompson melted the butter in a wide pan, and Lucy slid the flour in, stirring. The mixture bubbled and turned the color of wet sand. "Now the milk goes in slowly," he said, "and then the cheese. If it clumps, you'll know."

Lucy poured a thin stream of milk and stirred, and there, right at the edge of the whisk, she saw it: one small stubborn lump. She frowned at it. Was the lump there because she had poured too fast, or because the flour hadn't cooked long enough, or something else entirely? She couldn't see inside the lump to find out. She would have to deduce it from what she could see.

She thought for a moment, then asked Mr. Thompson for a fresh pan. If the problem was her pouring, she could fix it without starting over; if the problem was the flour itself, a new batch would lump too. It was a simple test. She weighed fifty grams of butter and fifty grams of flour again, but this time she let the flour cook in the melted butter a full minute longer, until it smelled faintly like toast, before a single drop of milk went in. Then she poured even more slowly than before, whisking the whole time, and the sauce came together smooth as paint.

"Look at that," Kieran said, leaning over her shoulder. "Not one lump."

"That's exceptional," Rory said, already reaching for the grated cheese.

Lucy stirred the cheese in and watched it melt into a glossy golden river. She ladled it over a bowl of pasta, held up the spoon, and let the sauce ribbon down in one unbroken strand.

"Next Saturday," she said, "I want to try it with pepper."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
story:
The lights went out at 7:03, right in the middle of Justin's homework, and the whole house went dark except for the microwave clock, which blinked a smug little nothing. Justin found his flashlight in the junk drawer, where it had been thriving between a dead battery and a rubber band ball since last summer. "Power cut," his dad announced from the hallway, as if anyone needed the update. "I'll find candles. Don't open the fridge, everything in there is precious."

Through his bedroom window, Justin noticed the garage next door glowing faintly. Mr. Tesfaye's garage. A generator was humming in there, and Mr. Tesfaye was dragging a second one, still in its box, toward the open garage door. That seemed odd. Justin had read a whole safety pamphlet in the dentist's waiting room once, because there was nothing else to do and the magazines were from 2015. He remembered the big bold warning on the back page word for word: run generators outdoors only, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.

He pulled on his boots and ran next door. "Mr. Tesfaye! Wait!"

Mr. Tesfaye looked up, holding an extension cord like a lasso. "Justin! Come to borrow electricity? I'm setting up the backup. The fridge has my wife's prescriptions in it, cold medicine, the works. Can't let it all go warm."

"It's just, you can't run it in the garage," Justin said. "Generators have to stay outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never inside a house or a garage. It was on a whole pamphlet."

"In the garage? It's raining out there."

"So put it under the eaves at the far end of the yard," Justin said. "Is that feasible? Far from every door and window?"

Mr. Tesfaye scratched his chin, looked at his generator, then at the far corner of the yard, then at the pamphlet-memory of Justin's face. "Feasible. Barely. You'll help me carry the cord."

They hauled the extension cord across the wet grass together, and Mr. Tesfaye set the generator by the fence, as far from any door or window as his property allowed. It grumbled to life in the drizzle like a giant disgruntled lawnmower. "You," he said, pointing at Justin with the empty box, "are getting the first slice of pizza when my oven's back. Gas oven. Still works, no electricity needed."

"Deal," said Justin. "But my dad says I can't open our fridge, so honestly I would've settled for a sandwich."

Back home, the lights flicked on at 8:15, and the microwave clock blinked 12:00 like it had no idea what it had missed. Justin's dad came in holding a candle and a fork. "Power's back. Pizza night?"

Justin was already lacing his boots. "Sort of. We're eating next door."

"Best prescription I've heard all night," his dad said, and grabbed his coat.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A novel's theme is usually implied rather than stated outright, so readers infer it from what the characters do and what happens to them.
story:
Samantha flopped into the reading nook with her library copy of The Long Walk Home, a pad of sticky notes, and a mission. Mr. Perera had said their paragraph was due Monday: state the theme and back it up with a quotation. Easy, she thought. She would just find the sentence where the book said the moral.

She flipped pages, hunting. "Mia learned that..." Nothing. "The lesson of her journey was..." Nothing. By chapter six she had covered the endpapers in sticky notes and found exactly zero sentences that came out and said what the book was about. "You're hiding it," she told the novel, which was ridiculous, because books couldn't hide anything. Could they?

She texted Elina. Do authors put the theme in italics somewhere? Elina replied with a row of question marks and then: Winter says you're supposed to guess it. Samantha frowned at that. Guessing felt like cheating on a test. But then a more logical idea germinated in her mind, slow at first and then all at once: maybe the theme wasn't a sentence at all. Maybe it was in what Mia did, what happened to her, the pattern running underneath the whole story.

Time to test it. Samantha made a list. Mia gave her seat on the bus to the old man. Mia lost the race but kept running anyway to finish with her brother. Mia's father forgave her at the end even though she never asked. She read the list three times, feeling a flicker of skepticism that faded fast. Every single thing Mia did came back to the same thing: kindness that costs you something. That was it. That was the theme, and the book had never once said it out loud.

She hunted one more time, this time for proof, and found it in chapter eleven. Mia's grandmother says, "Doing the right thing never comes free, but it's still the right thing." Samantha copied it, underlined the theme she had dug out of the story herself, and grinned at the ceiling of the nook.

Then she texted Elina: Guessing is allowed. Actually it's not guessing, it's detective work. Tell Winter I'm bringing sticky notes for both of you Monday.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
Marcus's new phone arrived on a Tuesday, and by the following Tuesday it had stopped loading things. This seemed unfair, since the whole point of a phone was loading things.

At Axel's house, Axel took the phone, looked at the little grey bar in the corner, and handed it back. "You used all your data," he said, as if announcing the weather. Marcus had not known data could run out. He had thought of it more like air. "My mom says I get ten gigabytes a month," Axel went on. "I made it three weeks once. You lasted, what, a week?"

Marcus sat on the floor of Axel's kitchen and thought about that. He had not done anything unusual, unless the bus counted. Every morning and every afternoon on the bus, he had watched videos, because the bus was forty minutes long and the videos were right there. At home, the phone used the Wi-Fi, and nothing happened. On the bus, no Wi-Fi, and something had happened, invisibly, a little at a time.

"Okay," Marcus said slowly. "So at home it's free, and on the bus it isn't. And videos are the expensive part." He borrowed Axel's phone, which still had data, and sent himself a text. One message, and the little counter barely moved, a number so small it looked like a rounding error. Then he played thirty seconds of a video and watched the number drop like a stone in a bucket. "That's it," he said. "Videos eat it. Texts barely touch it. It's like the difference between a grape and a whole grocery store." He had managed to isolate the cause in one afternoon, which felt almost scientific, and slightly too late.

From then on he texted on the bus and saved the videos for Wi-Fi at home, like a normal, non-rebellious citizen of the internet. His phone, a thin descendant of the brick his dad still carried, settled into quiet obedience.

On Friday, Ms. Ma kept him after class about a missing homework email. Marcus explained, honestly, that his data was gone. She looked at him for a long moment.

"So you watched videos on the bus all week," she said.

"Once or twice," said Marcus.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
Olivia had been waiting for this game all week, and now the last minute was ticking down with the score tied. She sat cross-legged on the living room rug between Rory and Frances, a bowl of popcorn balanced on her knees, while her dad paced behind the couch like a caged animal. The Harriers were playing at home tonight, and the whole crowd on the TV screen was roaring in blue and gold.

When the Harriers scored the winning goal, the living room exploded. Rory leapt onto the couch cushions, and Frances high-fived Olivia so hard her palm stung. But then, mid-celebration, Rory flopped back down and frowned. "They only won because they were at home. Put them in another stadium and they lose. I bet."

"No way," Frances said, grabbing another handful of popcorn. "They're just the better team."

Olivia chewed on that while the players hugged on screen. She remembered the last Harriers game she had watched with her grandfather, a road game two states away, when they had lost by two. She remembered being surprised, because they had looked unstoppable that whole month. Her grandfather had shaken his head and said the crowd could carry a team. At the time she had wondered if that was actually true, or just something grandparents said.

Now she wanted proof. She borrowed her dad's phone and searched for how often home teams win, expecting Rory to be mostly wrong. Instead, the numbers stared back at her: in most major sports, home teams win more than half their games. She read the phrase printed at the top of the page out loud. "It's called home advantage."

"So I was right?" Rory said, sitting up.

"Half right," Olivia said. "It's real, but it's not everything. The Harriers still had to score." She thought for a second, then went on, because an idea was forming. "We can speculate all night about whether they'd win away, but we don't have to guess. Their next game is on the road, Saturday. My dad already said we're watching it here."

Frances pointed at the screen, where the Harriers coach was giving an interview. "He looks worried about something."

Olivia grinned and hugged the popcorn bowl. "Saturday," she said, "we find out."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
The classroom store opened every Friday at lunch, and Mya ran the cash box because Mr. Johansson said she was the only one who could count change without demolishing the supply of receipts. Last week the sparkle pens had cost one quarter. This week a folded note appeared on Mya's desk before the bell, in Baby's round, careful handwriting: "Dear Mya, please save me a sparkle pen. My mom said the ones at the store went up to two dollars so she bought plain ones instead, and a plain pen is not the same, it is a random sad stick. I will pay anything. Baby." Mya smoothed the note flat and looked at the store shelf, where exactly six sparkle pens remained out of a box of forty.

When Mr. Johansson announced the new price of one dollar, because the box was nearly gone, a murmur went around the room. Vincenzo pushed to the front and studied the shelf. "A dollar for sparkle? What about those?" He pointed at the plain blue pens, the ones that had sat unsold for a month, priced at a quarter. "They write the same," he said, and bought two. So did the girl behind him, and then three more kids, until the plain pens, a substitute that did the same job, had a line in front of them and the sparkle pens did not.

Mya watched the pattern and thought about last month, when she had raised the gum-shaped erasers to fifty cents just because she liked them, and nobody bought any until she brought the price back down. She had blamed the erasers then. Now she wondered if she had blamed the wrong thing. Between customers she counted the plain pens twice, and the stack kept shrinking.

By the end of lunch the plain pens were gone entirely, sold out for the first time ever, and one sparkle pen sat alone on the shelf. Mya picked it up and turned it in the window light, where the glitter scattered like a tiny prism. She set it inside her desk, then took it out again, then set it back inside.

She found Baby in the hallway and held up the pen. "One dollar, like I promised Mr. Johansson," she said, "or you can owe me."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A standard AA battery provides about 1.5 volts.
story:
John spread the parts across the kitchen table: two bulbs, a plastic switch, a tangle of wire, and every AA battery he could find in the junk drawer. Mr. Crowchild had announced it that afternoon. "Tomorrow morning, each of you demonstrates a working circuit and explains why the bulb lights. No exceptions." John had until breakfast.

He clipped a wire to one battery, snapped the switch closed, and stared at the bulb. Nothing. Not a flicker. His little sister's erosion poster, still drying on the counter, curling at one corner, seemed to mock him with its neatly labeled canyon. He tried a different wire. Still dark.

He called Harley, who arrived five minutes later with Giselle and a box of batteries held shut with durable silver tape. "My grandpa says electricity is invisible," Harley said, peeling the tape with his teeth. "You can't perceive it moving. You can only see what it does."

"That's the problem," John said. "The wire's fine. The bulb's fine. So what's missing?" He turned the battery over in his fingers and read the tiny print on its side. "Wait. A standard AA battery provides about 1.5 volts." He checked the bulb package. "This bulb needs three volts."

Giselle grabbed a second battery and lined it up nose to tail in John's holder. "So two of them together," she said. John connected the last wire, took a breath, and pressed the switch. The bulb glowed a warm, steady yellow.

"It's a loop," John said, tracing the path with his finger. "Battery, wire, switch, bulb, back to the battery. Break the loop anywhere and it goes dark." He flicked the switch off and on three times, watching the light obey, and grinned. "Mr. Crowchild is going to think we're geniuses."

"Two geniuses and one battery supplier," Harley said, and held out his hand for a high five.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
The ball came off Matheo's foot and smacked Simon in the back of the head, and Simon was sure it was on purpose, because they had argued an hour before about whose turn it was to use the good goal.

"That was deliberate," Simon said, walking over to the goal line where Matheo stood.

"It wasn't. Ask Josiah."

Josiah shrugged from midfield. "I wasn't watching."

"Convenient," said Simon. He picked up the ball and compress it under his arm so Matheo couldn't take the next kick. The whole thing had started when Matheo said Simon's foul in the first game was obvious, and Simon said the ref's calls were subjective anyway, and now every hit and shove felt aimed.

Then Simon looked down. The grass near the goal line was darker than the rest, and his own sneaker slid an inch when he shifted his weight. A sprinkler head by the fence was still dripping. He put the ball down, walked to the spot where Matheo had kicked, and pressed his heel into the ground. It slid too, the same way.

"You slipped," Simon said. "Right here. It's slick from the sprinkler."

"I told you," Matheo said. "I was aiming for the goal and my plant foot went sideways."

"Show me."

Matheo put his foot on the dark patch and slid it forward, almost losing his balance again. Josiah came over and tried it too, and then Simon tried it, and all three of them stood there sliding their shoes in the wet grass like penguins.

"Okay," Simon said. He thought about how fast he had decided it was deliberate, without checking anything. "I decided you meant it before I even looked at the ground."

"That's like the tray thing in Ms. Rossi's class," Josiah said. "Hostile attribution bias. When something's unclear and you just assume the person meant to hurt you."

"Yeah," Simon said. "That."

Matheo rolled the ball to Simon with the flat of his hand. "Your kick."

Simon set the ball on the dry side of the patch and backed up three steps.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: In front crawl, the body rolls from side to side with each stroke, and the breath is taken as part of that roll rather than by twisting the neck alone.
story:
"Twenty-five metres, one length, no stopping," Beatrice announced to the whole community pool, which was really just Brittany, Imran, and a toddler in the shallow end. "Today is the day."

Last summer, a wasp had invaded her lemonade, her towel, and finally her hair at a birthday party, and she'd stood frozen in the shallow end while everyone else splashed to safety. That was the day she'd decided to learn front crawl properly, and today she'd complete a whole length with side breathing. She hoped.

Her first attempt went fine for about six strokes. Then her neck began to ache, sharp and hot, like someone had poured molten metal along one side of it. She stopped, stood up in the chest-deep water, and rubbed it. Brittany was already swimming laps like a motorboat, because Brittany wanted to beat the pool record board before she turned twelve, and the record was 19 seconds for 25 metres, held by some legend named K. Okafor since 1998.

"You look like a robot having second thoughts," Imran called from the wall. He wasn't even trying to swim; he wanted to lifeguard someday, so he practiced spotting people who were struggling. Beatrice was, apparently, his favorite practice subject.

"It's my neck," she said. "Every time I breathe, I have to crank my head around, and it kills."

She watched Brittany swim toward them, and something snagged in her brain. Brittany's shoulders weren't flat like a raft. They tipped, first one side, then the other, rolling with each stroke, and her head turned with the roll, easy, like the breath was just part of the tipping. Beatrice wasn't tipping at all. She was lying flat and twisting only her neck, which explained the ache. It was like the difference between opening a door with your whole arm and opening it with two fingers.

"I'm going to roll," Beatrice declared.

"Very dramatic," said Imran.

She pushed off, and this time, as her right arm reached, she let her whole side roll up with it, and her mouth found air without craning. One breath, then the other side, rolling again. The far wall rushed at her, and she smacked it with both hands.

"Twenty-five metres!" Imran shouted, standing up on the wall like a lifeguard who had just spotted something wonderful. "You looked almost like Brittany!"

Brittany surfaced, gasping and delighted. "Twenty-two seconds. Not the record, but you," she said, pointing at Beatrice, "rolled your breath. Took me a whole summer to figure that out."

Mr. Swampy, the pool manager, wandered over with his clipboard. "Who needs the deep end unlocked?"

"Beatrice does," said Brittany. "She's earned it."

Beatrice looked at the deep end, then at her neck, which didn't hurt even a little. "Two lengths next," she said, and dove for the ladder.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
story:
Rosalie stood at the front of the language room with her poster of stick-figure family members and a drawing of a lop-eared rabbit named Biscuit. Mr. Reyes had asked each student to describe their family in French using full sentences, and she had practiced in the mirror until the words came out smooth. "J'ai un frère," she began. "Il s'appelle Marc. Et sa mère adore le lapin." She pointed at the rabbit and sat down, pleased.

Jayden raised his hand before Mr. Reyes could say anything. "Wait. Your brother's mother adores the rabbit? That's your mom, right? So why not say your mom?" Rosalie frowned. She had meant her mother, but she had attached the sentence to her brother, and now Jayden had heard something different. She checked her notes, and the words on the page looked exactly like what she had said. Both of them, she realized slowly, could be right at the same time.

She leaned toward Callen, who sat beside her and kept a neat chart of French words in the back of his notebook. "If I said sa mère about my brother, could it mean his mother or her mother?" Callen turned his chart toward her. "Either one. It depends on the thing owned, not who owns it." Rosalie tried it out in a whisper, pointing at a girl in the class and saying sa mère, then pointing at a boy and saying the same two words. Identical. The owner's side didn't matter at all.

She stood up again. "Mr. Reyes, may I try once more?" He nodded and gestured at the poster. "Ma mère adore le lapin," she said clearly, and this time Jayden nodded without confusion. Then, to test her idea, she added a sentence about her cousin Léa. "Sa mère a un chien," she said, and looked at Jayden. "Whose mother?" Jayden hesitated. "Léa's? You'd have to tell us." "That's the trick," Rosalie said. "You can't tell until you ask."

After class, Mr. Reyes stopped her at the door and said she could donate her poster to the classroom wall for the next group of beginners. Rosalie looked at her stick figures and thought the poster told less of a story than she had assumed, like a narrator leaving out one small thing on purpose. She pinned it up beside the door. Below the rabbit she wrote, in careful letters, "Demandez: whose?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Grandpa's house smelled like old newspapers and lemon polish, the way it always had, except nobody had polished anything for months. Anthony stood in the kitchen holding a plastic bag of small brooms, the kind you sweep a car dashboard with. His mother was loading a thermos of tea into a box, and Ms. Chukwu from next door had come over with a tin of shortbread, which she set on the counter without a word.

Anthony had a problem. He was supposed to sweep Grandpa's gravestone today, with his cousins Caden and Memphis, but he did not know what you were supposed to say while you did it, or whether you were supposed to say anything at all. At the last funeral he had only been eleven and had stood in the back and copied whatever his father did. This time his father had handed him the bag of brooms and said, "You're older now," which was not instructions.

At the cemetery the morning sun made the granite radiate heat against his palm when he touched the stone. Caden wanted to get the sweeping done fast so they could catch tadpoles in the creek behind the fence before lunch. Memphis, who was ten and took everything literally, wanted to know exactly how many sweeps counted as clean.

Memphis pointed at other families farther down the hill, who were sweeping stones too, and pulling weeds, and setting out oranges and little cakes. "Why is everybody here today?" she asked. "It's not a weekend."

"It's called Qingming," Caden said, checking his phone. "It's usually on April fourth or fifth, and families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings. Grandpa used to do it for his mother. Remember? He'd take the train every spring."

Anthony did remember, suddenly and completely: Grandpa with a bucket and a folded towel, coming back with mud on his shoes in early April, saying he had been "tidying up for Grandma Wu." Anthony had always thought he meant a living person. He had never once asked. That was the part that sat wrong in his stomach, so he decided to test the fix he had thought of on the drive over. He took out his phone and recorded a minute of himself talking to the stone, telling Grandpa about the science fair, about how he had built the electromagnet from an old doorbell because the doorbell itself was obsolete, and about how the magnet's strength came from the coil and the iron core, not from any magic. Grandpa would have argued about the magic part. Anthony saved the file and labeled it "Qingming, first one."

Then he handed brooms to Caden and Memphis. Caden swept fast and sloppy so he could get to the creek, but Memphis swept in careful rows, counting under her breath, and Anthony set an orange and a piece of Ms. Chukwu's shortbread at the base of the stone, next to the little bronze marker whose edges were worn to a dull shine, some alloy gone soft-looking with age. He crouched and ran his thumb along the letters of Grandpa's name.

"Two hundred," Memphis announced, standing back. "That's clean."

"Good," Anthony said. "Same time next April."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
The group chat had been quiet all afternoon until Flora posted a photo of her new bedroom, curtains open, sunlight across the bed. "Finally painted!" she wrote, and eleven people replied with hearts. Willow enlarged the picture to envy the window seat properly, then noticed something odd. When she tapped the little "i" at the bottom of the image, a screen slid up with numbers and, underneath them, a map. The map showed a pin, and the pin sat on Flora's actual street, right where her house was.

Willow typed, deleted, and typed again. "Flora, where did you send this from?" Flora answered fast. "My room, why?" Willow's stomach tightened. She tapped her own last photo, a picture of Sara at the bakery, and checked its details. There was her map pin too, marking the exact corner where they'd stood. She remembered that her location services had been on that day, because the maps app had been guiding her mom's car. She tested one more thing, switching location off and sending Flora a photo of her shoe. This time the details showed no pin at all.

"That's called EXIF metadata," Flora said when Willow explained what she'd found. "Sara told me once. Hidden data inside the file." Sara herself joined the chat a minute later, breathless. "Wait, you can see WHERE my photo was taken?" She pasted the bakery picture and checked it, and the three of them watched the pin come up together, silent for a moment before the typing bubbles started racing.

The problem arrived before they solved anything. Someone named Duckfan99, whom none of them had added, had been in the chat since Tuesday, added by a link someone forwarded. Nobody had thought about it. Willow scrolled back and found that Duckfan99 had replied "nice street" to Flora's bedroom photo, and then, worse, had posted a screenshot of that same photo's detail screen, pin circled in red.

"I'm leaving the group," Flora wrote, which surprised Willow, because Flora usually wanted to stay in every chat ever invented. But Willow had a different idea, and she argued for it with the most objective message she could manage: kick the stranger out, turn off location, strip the pins from their old photos, and stay. Mr. Rowe had once shown her class how to report an account, and she dug up the citation for it now, the school's tech safety page, and pasted the link. Within ten minutes Flora had removed Duckfan99, the report had gone through, and the three of them sat in the rebuilt chat, sending plain, pinless photos of their dinners. "Okay," Flora typed at last. "Staying. But Willow checks everything from now on."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: For most swimmers, most of the forward push in front crawl comes from the arms, while the kick mainly keeps the legs high and the body balanced.
story:
The outdoor court behind the rec centre was Wyatt's thinking spot, and today he had a lot to think about. He sat on the warm pavement, still smelling of chlorine, bouncing a basketball in a slow rhythm while his friends shot hoops at the other end. Tomorrow was the swim test, twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, and today at the pool he had barely made it ten metres before his legs turned to cement.

"You look like you lost a game nobody else was playing," Sofie said, jogging over with the ball under her arm. She'd been in the lane beside him at the pool. "I saw you out there. You were kicking like crazy."

"That's the thing," Wyatt said. He bounced the ball harder. "I kicked the whole way and I still sank and got tired. It doesn't make sense. Kicking should move me forward, right? More kick, more speed."

Kassidy wandered over too, sweat shining on her forehead. "My cousin swims on a club team. She says her coach tells her to kick less, not more."

Wyatt stopped bouncing. That was weird. Why would a coach say that? He thought about the fast swimmer he'd seen in the next lane, gliding smooth as a whale, barely making a splash with his feet. Then he thought about himself, churning the water white and going nowhere. Maybe the kick wasn't what propelled the swimmer at all. Maybe it did something else, like keeping his legs up so they didn't drag him down. His arms, though, his arms had felt strong even when he was exhausted.

At the court, he grabbed his water bottle and lay on his stomach, arms stretched out on the pavement like he was reaching for a faraway wall. "Watch," he said. He pulled one arm back in a slow circle, then the other. "That's what the good swimmer was doing. Arms pulling water. His feet just stayed high and quiet, like a rudder, keeping him level."

"So your legs were sinking because you were saving them for kicking instead of using them to balance?" Kassidy asked.

"Something like that. The arms do the moving. The kick mainly keeps you flat." The insight felt so obvious now that he almost laughed.

The next evening at the pool, Wyatt pushed off the wall with a plan. Arms first, always arms. He breathed to the side the way he'd practised, one goggle in the water, one out, and let his legs flutter easy behind him instead of thrashing. At ten metres he wasn't tired. At fifteen the wall was still far away but his body felt long and light. His hand slapped the tiles at the far end and he stood up gasping, grinning through wet hair.

From the bleachers, Sofia cupped her hands and shouted, "Twenty-five metres! You did it!"

Wyatt raised one fist out of the water like a champion. "Arms and eggs!" he yelled back, breathless and delighted. "Tomorrow we celebrate with pizza and a rematch on the court!"

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
story:
Riley marched into the pharmacy behind her mom with a mission: new deodorant, because fifth grade had suddenly decided she needed it, and the hygiene aisle was calling her name. She had even worn her most sophisticated jacket, the one with the zippers, because today felt like a step toward being an actual teenager. She grabbed two different deodorants and held them up like trophies.

In the checkout line, she hitched up her jeans, and that's when she saw them. Thin, pale lines, a few of them, curved across her hips like tiny roads on a map. Her stomach dropped. She pulled her shirt down fast and checked whether the cashier was looking, then whether the man behind them was looking. Nobody was, but that didn't matter, because something was clearly happening to her skin.

"Mom," she whispered. "Can we look at bandage stuff?"

Her mom steered the cart to aisle four while Riley pretended to compare prices on gauze. "So," she said, keeping her voice low. "If you had lines on your skin, from like a scratch, what would happen?"

"A scratch would fade in a week or two. Why?"

Riley pulled up the edge of her shirt just enough. Her mom leaned in, then smiled in that infuriating calm way. "Those are stretch marks. Fast growth during puberty often causes them. They're really common, and they usually fade over time."

"Puberty?" Riley said it too loud, and a woman at the end of the aisle glanced over. Riley lowered her voice. "So I'm growing too fast for my skin?"

"That's one way to think about it. Your body's just moving quicker than usual."

Riley did the math right there, holding a box of adhesive bandages she suddenly didn't need. She had grown two shoe sizes since August. Her jeans from September didn't button anymore. The lines were on her hips, which was exactly where all that growing had to stretch. It wasn't a rash. It wasn't a bug. It was a receipt from a growth spurt, stamped right on her skin. She tested the idea one more way: she remembered her cousin's knees last summer, purplish lines after a huge growth spurt, and how they were fainter by Christmas. Fading over time. It fit.

She put the bandages back and jogged to catch her mom at the register. "So next summer they might be way lighter?"

"Probably."

Riley set the deodorant on the counter and grinned at her reflection in the pharmacy window, tall and growing taller by the minute. "Then I'm getting the extra-strength one," she said. "No point in being subtle about it."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: One degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance.
story:
"Grandma Rosa's hometown is four degrees south of us," Kayla announced, flapping the trail map so hard it crackled. "I figured it out last night. Four little lines on the map, Charleigh. That's all that's between her village and this trail."

Charleigh, who was busy extracting a pebble from her sneaker, looked up. "Lines mean what, exactly? Like, miles?"

"That's the thing." Kayla tapped the thin curved lines running across the folded paper. "Mr. Barrett said one degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance. So I just count the degrees and multiply. Four degrees is about 444 kilometers. Or 276 miles. I did it both ways because I wanted to see if they matched, and they do!"

They were climbing the switchback trail behind the school, the one that smelled like pine sap and last year's damp leaves. Mr. Barrett walked ahead with the first-aid kit bouncing on his hip, and Leana trudged behind them muttering a campfire song under her breath, one stanza at a time, trying to memorize it before the overnight trip on Friday. "Second stanza keeps escaping me," she groaned. "It's like a fish."

Kayla hardly heard her. She had a plan, and plans made her feel like a rocket on a launchpad. "Okay, here's my test," she said, stopping at the overlook where the whole valley opened up, hazy and blue. "Grandma says her village is south of us, about a five-hour bus ride. If the bus goes, say, eighty kilometers an hour, five hours is roughly 400 kilometers. My map math said 444. That's close. If it works, the degree trick is real."

She smoothed the map on a flat rock and counted again, one finger, one line at a time. Charleigh leaned over her shoulder, breathing trail-mix breath. "You're sure it's four? Not, like, three and a half?"

"Grandma wrote the number on a postcard. I checked twice."

Mr. Barrett wandered back, glanced at the map, and raised an eyebrow. "Somebody's been reading latitude lines. Very unconventional behavior for a snack break."

"It's not unconventional, it's math," Kayla said, grinning. "And it works. The bus time and the degrees mostly agree, so the distance between us and Grandma Rosa is about four degrees, about 444 kilometers, about 276 miles. Can I write to her and tell her exactly where she is?"

Leana popped up between them, sand on her knees. "Wait, can you do it for my aunt in the north? Count her degrees too?"

"Give me a map and a snack," Kayla said, "and I'll give you her distance by the time we reach the top." She folded the paper with a snap and started up the trail at a run.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The standard tuning pitch for the A above middle C is 440 vibrations per second, an international standard known as A440.
story:
Victor stood in the wings of the community theater, holding his violin like it might bite him. He was third on the program for the school concert, and his bow hand would not stop shaking.

"It's just three minutes of music," said Valentina, peeking through the curtain. "You've practiced the piece two hundred times."

"That's the problem," Victor whispered. "Two hundred times with my tuner app, and the thing still confuses me." He pulled out his phone and showed her the screen, where a needle swung back and forth. When he played his open A string, the app flashed the number 440. He had stared at that number all week. Why 440 and not 400, or 500? It felt like a locked door at the frontier of some secret nobody had told him.

Blanche poked her head in from the prop room. "Mr. Hoang tuned the theater piano an hour ago," she said. "I watched him. He played one note over and over and stared at his own phone."

Victor's heart jumped. If the piano's A and his A matched, maybe every instrument in the whole world agreed on the same number. He slipped onstage during the break, played his open A against the piano's A, and heard the two notes lock together like puzzle pieces. His app still read 440. So it wasn't just his app being fussy. The A above middle C vibrated 440 times every second, and that was the standard everywhere, like an international agreement. He found Valentina in the wings. "It's called A440," she said with a shrug. "My cousin's orchestra uses it too. Same number in Brazil."

Somehow knowing that made the shaking stop. If every violinist on Earth tuned to the same A, then he wasn't alone up there; he was part of one enormous, invisible orchestra. He had wanted to postpone his performance until the spring concert, but now he told the stage manager he was ready. Blanche, who had insisted he would freeze, changed her mind too and gave him a thumbs-up from the light booth.

He walked out, raised his bow, and played his A, steady and true at 440.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
story:
The car smelled like coffee and rain, and Camille's mom kept checking the clock on the dashboard because they had exactly eleven minutes to pick up Sarah-Eve and still make it to school before the late bell. Camille sat in the back with her gym bag between her feet, and she was thinking about a problem she had never had before this year: her gym shirt.

Yesterday, after running laps in Ms. López's class, she had pulled the shirt out of her bag at home and it had smelled, well, not good. She had sniffed her own arm right after the laps, when she was still dripping, and there had been almost nothing there. So the sweat itself was not the problem. She was sure of that, because she had tested it.

"It was Romeo who figured it out for me," she said out loud, mostly to the window.

"Figured what out?" her mom asked, braking for a yellow light.

Camille flashed back to Tuesday, sitting on the gym bleachers while Ms. López set out cones. Romeo had been holding a stick of deodorant and staring at it like it was a message from space. "I never needed this before," he'd said. "My older cousin told me it's because of puberty. There are glands in your armpits that only turn on then, and fresh sweat from them has almost no smell. The smell comes later, when bacteria on your skin break the sweat down." He'd waved the deodorant. "Bacteria. Like tiny decomposers, eating my sweat. That is the grossest thing I've ever learned."

In the car, Camille explained her plan. If the smell came from bacteria doing their work over time, then the smart move was to stop them before they started. Deodorant in the morning was like locking the door before the thieves arrived, not after. It wasn't complicated, but testing it day after day would be tedious, which is why she wanted proof fast.

"There's Sarah-Eve," her mom said, pulling up to the curb.

Camille rolled down the window. "Quick question. Do you wear deodorant before gym or after?"

Sarah-Eve leaned in, buckling her seatbelt. "Before. Why?"

"Testing something." Camille pulled the fresh stick out of her gym bag and held it up like a trophy. "Five minutes to the bell. Pass it back after you're done with it."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Chiaroscuro, an Italian word meaning 'light-dark', is the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid.
story:
Lea sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a mandarin orange, a lamp, and a blank page, because Mr. Romano had made the sphere assignment mandatory: draw a ball with a light source, and make it look solid enough to pick up. Her first three attempts looked like flat gray planets. The orange, sitting in the lamplight, refused to cooperate; it had a bright spot near the top, a darker curve along the bottom, and a long smudged shadow stretching across the table like the orange's evil twin.

Subhan had come over to help, mostly by eating the second orange. "It's like the shadow is telling on the light," he said, pointing at the smudge. "Wherever it points, that's where the light came from." Lea frowned. The cast shadow leaned away from the lamp, and its edge was crisp near the orange but fuzzy at the far end, as if the shadow got tired and forgot its own shape. She tested his idea by moving the lamp slowly to the left, watching the shadow swing right like a compass needle that had been waiting all along for someone to turn it.

Then her grandmother came downstairs and slid an old art book across the table, the kind with paint flecks on the cover. "You two were whispering about a museum trip last week," she said. "There's a word in here you'll like." Lea flipped through it and stopped at a painting of a bowl of fruit that looked so round she felt she could tip it over. Beside it was a printed label from a gallery wall, and one word stood out: chiaroscuro.

"Chiaroscuro," Subhan read aloud, chewing. "It's Italian. It means 'light-dark.' It's the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid."

Lea stared at the bowl in the book, then at her orange. The painter hadn't drawn a gray ball; the painter had dragged everything near the light almost white and let everything far from it sink into near black, and the fruit swelled out of the canvas because of the gap between the two. She picked up her softest pencil, pushed the dark side of her sphere as dark as it would go, and pressed a tiny window of white paper at the highlight, leaving it untouched, a hole where the light lived. When she added the cast shadow, darker and harder-edged near the base, the sphere lifted right off the page.

"That looks like you could bowl with it," Subhan said, and held out his half-peeled orange as if it were a trophy. Lea laughed, rolled her drawing into a tube, and set it upright in the empty fruit bowl, where the lamplight threw a real shadow against it, wrapping around the paper like a signed testimony that at last, she had gotten it right.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Luca stood at the back of the cultural center's big hall, holding a box of marigolds his mother had asked him to carry. Rows of tables were being turned into altars, and the whole room smelled like burnt sugar and candle wax. He had never been to a Día de los Muertos celebration before, and he was not sure what he was supposed to do with any of it.

"Luca, over here," called Ms. Morin, his art teacher, who organized the event. She pointed to a three-tiered table covered with purple paper. "This is our class's ofrenda." Luca set the box down and looked around at the other altars. Every single one had photographs on it, and candles, and little clay skeletons laughing and dancing. His class's ofrenda had the paper and the flowers but no photos at all.

"Why do they all have pictures?" he asked Mathilde, who was folding paper flowers nearby. She shrugged. Morgane came rushing over from the craft table, holding a small framed photo of an old man with white hair and a wooden cane.

"It's my bisabuelo," Morgane said. "My great-grandfather. He came from Oaxaca. My mom said to bring it tonight because the celebration honors family members who have died, and the altars are how we invite them back to visit."

Luca looked at the empty top tier of their table. "So everybody in our class could bring a photo tomorrow? The celebration goes on through November first and second, right? That's what the schedule says." Morgane nodded. "Then tonight we put your photo up, and tomorrow we ask everyone else."

He was a little embarrassed to ask the whole class, in case someone thought it was strange, but Ms. Morin overheard him and said, "That's the best idea I've heard all evening." So the next afternoon, Luca stood at the front of his classroom with Morgane, and they explained that anyone who wanted could bring a picture of a grandparent or a great-grandparent, or even a pet. He held up a photo of his own grandfather, who had died two years before, standing in front of a bakery with flour on his hands.

By the last day, the ofrenda looked nothing like the bare table it had been. There were eleven photos, four candles, a plate of pan de muerto that Mathilde's aunt had baked, and a toy fire truck that Luca had brought because his grandfather had driven a delivery van and loved anything with wheels. Visitors to the center stopped and looked, and one woman pressed her hands together in front of the photos.

"You know," Ms. Morin said quietly, standing beside him, "I was worried nobody would come to our altar. You gave it a reason to be here."

Luca lit one more candle and set it beside his grandfather's picture, watching the flame lean sideways in the draft from the open door.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Reflected light is light bouncing back from the table onto a sphere's shadow side; it is lighter than the core shadow but always darker than the lit side.
story:
Ms. Joshi set a white ball on the table under one lamp and said, "Today we make it look round on flat paper." Livia squinted at the ball, at the bright spot near the top, at the dark curve underneath. She wanted her drawing to look solid enough to pick up, and she pressed hard with her pencil to get there fast.

She shaded the whole lower half as dark as her pencil would go, then looked again. Something was off. Next to her, Delphine was doing the opposite, rubbing her eraser along the bottom edge of her sphere until the paper shone almost white. "I read that the shadow side isn't all dark," Delphine said happily. Livia leaned over and frowned. Delphine's ball had a bright spot on top and a pale rim along the bottom, as if two lamps were aimed at it from opposite directions.

"There's only one lamp," Livia said. "So the bottom can't be that light. But it isn't all black either." She held her pencil at arm's length and compared it against the ball. The bottom edge of the shadow side was a little lighter than the middle of the shadow, but clearly darker than anything on the lit side. She decided to test it. She shaded the center of the shadow darkest of all, then lightened her pressure toward the bottom edge, keeping that rim well darker than the top. When she propped the drawing beside the ball, it finally looked like one lamp was doing all the work.

"Mine looks like it has two light sources," Delphine said, her eraser hovering.

"Make the bottom edge lighter than the middle of the shadow, but still darker than the lit side," Livia said. "Ms. Joshi called that reflected light this morning. Light bounces back from the table onto the shadow side." Delphine redid her rim with a careful, gentle stroke, and her sphere turned from a flat cookie into something you could hold. Across the table Elias was hiding a smile behind his hand because his own ball had come out shaped like an egg, and Livia slid her spare pencil, a softer one, toward him without a word.

"Careful with that eraser," she told Delphine. "Keep rubbing and the paper will erode right through." Ms. Joshi walked past their table and tapped Delphine's drawing once. "That's a good sphere," she said. "Remember, it's not a metaphor for anything today. It's just light on a ball." Livia laughed, then turned back to add the soft cast shadow stretching from under her sphere across the table, a smear of gray, transparent where it thinned at the edge, dark where it met the ball. "Hold it still," she said, sliding the drawing next to the real one. "Which one is which?"

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.
story:
The sun was already hot on the barn roof when Chloe climbed the ladder with her sketchpad. She had promised Ms. Lombardi she would document a full food chain from the farm for the science fair, starting with grass and ending with the hawk that circled the north field every afternoon. She drew grass, then a grasshopper, then a mouse, then the hawk, and she felt pretty good about it until her friend Dash came huffing up the ladder with a tablet under his arm.

"You have to watch this," he said. "It's about creatures at the bottom of the ocean. Tube worms as tall as your arm, and crabs, and these fish nobody had ever seen, all living where sunlight can't reach. Zero light. Totally dark." He pressed play and let the tablet rest on the shingles between them. A narrator's voice said that in 1977, scientists in a submersible called Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.

Chloe stared at the screen. "That can't be right," she said. "Every food chain starts with the sun. That's the whole rule. Ms. Lombardi even said so." Dash shrugged and scrolled back so she could watch again. The screen showed pale crabs swarming around a smoking black chimney on the seafloor, and Chloe thought about her drawing, with its neat arrow from the sun to the grass. If the rule was wrong, then her poster was wrong, and the science fair was in three days.

That night she wrote to her cousin Robin, who loved ocean stuff.

Dear Robin, she wrote. Does every food chain really start with the sun? Dash showed me a documentary about the Alvin submarine in 1977, with vent animals living in complete darkness. The bacteria there use chemicals from the vents instead of sunlight. Is that a legitimate food chain or some weird exception? If it's real, I have to change my whole poster. Please answer fast. Chloe.

Robin's reply came the next morning: Legitimate! The ocean floor is full of them. Check whether sunlight is really the necessary variable, or just the one you can see.

Chloe taped a second strip of paper to her poster. On the left, the sun shone down on the farm chain. On the right, in dark blue marker, she drew a vent chimney and its bacteria, crabs above them, and a question mark at the top where a predator would be. She also added a folded flap over the mouse in the farm chain, and when Ms. Lombardi asked what it was, Chloe lifted it to reveal blank paper.

"If the mice disappear, the hawk loses its food," she said. "I'm testing whether the chain still works with one link gone."

Ms. Lombardi leaned closer to the blue side of the poster. "And this one starts with what, exactly?"

"Chemicals," Chloe said. "Not sunlight. The sun isn't the only beginning."

Dash grinned from the back of the room and gave the poster two thumbs up.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
story:
The playground had gone soft with late afternoon light, and Maeva sat on the low wall by the fence, her left arm resting in her lap like a question she could not answer. The cast had been white when the nurse wrapped it, but yesterday Maeva had chosen bright green for the new layer, and now Kale was drawing a row of tiny frogs along it. "Green was a bold choice," he said. "Heath said neon casts are controversial. He thinks they're too loud."

"They're not controversial," Maeva said. "They're just green." Her real worry was not the color. Something inside the cast itched, deep down where her fingers could not reach, and she had a theory about it. She had noticed the itch was worst right after PE, when she sweated, and almost gone in the morning. She reasoned it must be moisture trapped against her skin, though she could not see under the plaster to check. So she had a plan: today she would keep the arm completely dry and see if the itch stayed away.

Heath dropped onto the wall beside them, shaking a water bottle. "How did people even fix broken arms before casts?" he asked. "Did they just walk around with flopping arms forever?"

Maeva frowned. She had read a poster in the clinic waiting room while the doctor worked on her arm, mostly because there was nothing else to look at. "No. This Dutch army surgeon, Antonius Mathijsen, invented the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published how to do it in 1852. Before that nobody used this exact method." Heath looked at the cast with new respect, as if it had suddenly become older than the school.

At PE, Maeva sat out and kept her arm still and dry, holding it away from the sprinkler Ms. Anderson was using to water the flowerbeds by the gate. By the end of the hour the itch had faded to almost nothing, which meant her theory about trapped moisture was probably right, though she would test it again tomorrow to be sure. On the walk home she stopped at the corner store, bought a small towel with her pocket money, and tucked it carefully inside her backpack. "For drying off," she told Kale, "and for hygiene, so the skin under there stays clean."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: If a price is held below the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers will offer, and the result is a shortage.
story:
The note from Mr. Doyle was taped to the gym door on Monday morning. "Class store opens Friday at lunch. Bring your product and your price. Signed, Mr. Doyle." Zack read it twice, then ran to find Kira and Sameer, who were already arguing by the water fountain.

"Strawberry cups," Sameer said. "My mom gets flats of them in summer for almost nothing. That's the whole reason I picked them." Kira frowned and pulled out her notebook. "But we're buying them in winter, Sameer. Winter strawberries cost way more. I looked it up last night." She showed him the numbers, and Zack felt his stomach tighten. If they charged what the berries cost them, nobody would buy.

Zack lay awake that night turning the problem over. Summer meant piles of strawberries everywhere, so prices sank. Winter meant almost none, so prices climbed. That part made sense. What he couldn't see was what would happen if they charged less than the berries were worth on Friday. He decided to test it, because a low price felt friendly, and friendly had to be good for business.

Friday came fast. They set up their table outside the cafeteria, and Sameer wrote "50 cents a cup" on a poster in thick red marker. The bell rang, and the line formed before Zack had even opened the cash box. Kids pressed forward, coins rattling. By the time Zack counted to three hundred seconds, the cups were gone, and behind the counter the table looked desolate, nothing left but empty trays and a smear of pink juice. The line stretched past the library, and the kids at the back were not smiling.

"You said fifty cents," a boy near the front complained. "I stood here the whole lunch for nothing." Kira stepped around the table and held up her hands. "We're really sorry. We'll bring more Monday, and we'll have enough, we promise." A few kids grumbled off toward the cafeteria, and one girl muttered that she'd been waiting since the bell. Zack watched them go and understood, all at once, what he had done. "We held our price below what the cups were really worth," he said quietly. "So buyers wanted more than we would offer. That's why we ran out." Sameer slumped against the table. "My dilemma is I want it cheap and I want there to be enough. Can't have both?"

Mr. Doyle walked over, counted the short, frustrated line, and raised an eyebrow at Zack. "Something you want to clarify for the class on Monday?" Zack picked up the empty tray and smiled. "Yeah. Strawberry economics. Two dollars a cup, and everybody gets one."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Maya set the mixing bowl on the picnic table and stared at the lump of dough inside it. Twenty minutes ago it had been a smooth little hill. Now it was still a smooth little hill, exactly the same size, while Jaida's dough in the next bowl had puffed up like a pillow.

"Why is yours rebellious?" Jaida asked, poking Maya's dough with one finger. It didn't spring back. "Mine's practically climbing out of the bowl."

Maya ran through her logic out loud. Same bag of flour, same packet of yeast, same spoonful of sugar. The only thing they had done differently was the water. Jaida had filled her jug from the big thermos of cool drinking water. Maya, in a hurry, had dipped hers from the pot that had been sitting on the camp stove. She pressed her palm against the side of her bowl. It was warm. Really warm, the kind of warm that would sting if you held your hand in it.

"Water too hot," she said slowly. "I think it did something to the yeast. Dead yeast can't eat the sugar, so it can't let out the gas that gets trapped in the dough as bubbles. No bubbles, no rising." She peeled open a corner of Jaida's dough and leaned close. Sure enough, tiny holes pocked the inside like a sponge. Her own dough, when she tore a piece open, was dense and smooth with no holes at all.

"So can you fix it?" Jaida asked. She wanted fresh bread before dinner, and the last of their trail snacks had dwindled to a sad handful of pretzels.

"There's one more yeast packet," Maya said. "I'll use the cold jug this time and warm it just a little with my finger in it."

They mixed a new batch together, and while they waited, Maya checked every five minutes until the surface of the dough trembled and swelled. Mr. Ivanova wandered past their site and lifted the cloth covering the bowls. "Smells like a bakery already," he said.
