activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United Kingdom, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay.
story:
Emilia stood at the back of the town hall with her cue cards shaking in her hand. Her class had been assigned to explain how a bill becomes a law, and Mr. Lewandowski had arranged for three students to present at the actual town meeting, in front of actual adults. Sullivan had drawn a poster of a bill travelling through committee rooms and debate chambers, and Miguel had built a cardboard Parliament, but Emilia had the speaking part, and she had discovered last night that she did not understand her own part at all.

"The bill goes to the House of Commons, and then to the House of Lords," she whispered to Miguel, "and then it becomes law." She frowned at her cards. "But what if the Lords just say no? Forever? Then nothing ever becomes law."

"Then say they can't," Miguel said, indifferent to the whole problem, as he taped a paper flag to a cardboard tower.

Last summer, she remembered, she had sat on her grandmother's porch during a visit to England, complaining that her town council had voted down a skate park. Her grandmother had laughed. "You think that's stubborn? In Britain, the upper house isn't even elected. But they can't hold everything up. The Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay." Emilia had been half listening then, more interested in her lemonade, but now the words came back whole.

She grabbed Miguel's arm. "That's the missing piece. The Lords can delay, but they can't block forever. About a year, and then the Commons can go ahead."

"You sure?" Miguel asked.

She wasn't sure, so she tested it. While the adults argued about the town budget, Emilia and Sullivan set up the cardboard Parliament on a folding table and simulated the whole thing, right there behind the coffee urn. Sullivan played the Lords and rejected everything with a lordly sniff. Miguel read a bill aloud. Emilia moved a paper clock around the tower, one printed month at a time, and at the twelfth month she pushed Sullivan's hand aside and marched the bill to the other end of the table. "Passed without your consent," she announced, quietly enough that only they could hear. Sullivan had insisted the Lords could veto anything they liked, and now he crossed his arms and admitted, "Fine. A year's delay, then it goes through. That's actually fair."

When Mr. Lewandowski called her name, Emilia walked to the microphone without the cards. She explained the committees, the votes, both houses. Then she held up the cardboard clock and said, "And if one house keeps saying no, it still isn't stuck. In the United Kingdom, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay." An old man in the front row, the one who had looked bored all evening, sat up straight and started to clap.

From the back, Miguel lifted the paper flag over the cardboard tower.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
The cast on Theodore's left arm itched in three places he couldn't reach, and the doctor's office smelled like the inside of a band-aid. She clipped his X-ray to the light board and pointed with her pen.

"Two bones in there," she said. "The radius is the one on your thumb side. The ulna is on your little-finger side."

"Which one did I break?" Theodore asked, leaning closer.

"The ulna. See the crack, right near the little-finger side? You caught yourself with your hand open when you fell off the bike."

Theodore studied the picture. Two pale stripes, side by side like train tracks, and one of them had a thin dark line through it, like a hair laid across the track. He wiggled his little finger inside the cast, then his thumb. One of them was connected to that cracked stripe. It was strange to think about: the bones were under the cast, under the skin, and he couldn't see them, but he could still reason out which was which.

At school the next day, Ms. Zhang rearranged his desk to accommodate the cast, and Eileen carried his tray at lunch without being asked. At recess he sat on the bench by the soccer field, keeping score. Adley flopped down beside him, sweating.

"It was inevitable you'd end up scorekeeper," Adley said. "You fall off one bike and suddenly you're the bench guy."

Theodore ignored that. He was watching Aiden from the other team, who had missed his last three passes. All three went to the left, and all three were too high. "His passes keep going the same wrong way," Theodore said. "That's not bad luck. That's a pattern."

"So? He's just terrible."

"Or something's making it happen." Theodore stood, cupped his hands around his mouth, and called down the field. "Hey! Check your shoe!"

Aiden stopped, looked down, and pulled a folded page of newspaper out of the heel of his left cleat. He stared at it, laughed, and held it up like evidence.

Adley shook his head slowly. "Okay. Bench guy is now detective guy." He patted the empty spot on the bench. "Sit. Tell me everything you see."

Theodore sat, pulled the scorecard onto his knee with his good hand, and said, "Watch the sweeper. She marks on instinct, but she always cheats to the right. Somebody's going to notice that."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
The house smelled like Grandma Ruth's lemon dish soap, even though she had been gone for nine days. Hailey stood in the kitchen holding the wooden spoon her grandmother had used for every batch of oatmeal cookies. In the living room, relatives were saying goodbye to the house itself before the sale sign went up tomorrow. Hailey had a problem she could not say out loud. She wanted to take the spoon home and use it, and she wanted to keep wearing Grandma's flowered apron, which she had already tied on that morning. But a magazine in the waiting room at the funeral home had said people needed to "move on" after a death, and she was not sure whether keeping things meant she was doing it wrong.

She decided to run a test. She put the apron and the spoon in a box marked DONATE, went outside, and sat on the porch steps to see how that felt. It felt like the day she had dropped her library book in the pond. She retrieved the apron within two minutes. The test had failed, which meant, if the magazine was right, that she was failing too.

Mr. Kobayashi, the neighbour from across the hedge, was watering his tomatoes. "Big day tomorrow," he said. Hailey told him about her test, and about the magazine. He wiped his hands on his shorts. "You could look up a book called Continuing Bonds," he said. "Ruth had it. 1996." Then he went back to his tomatoes, because he was a man who said things once and stopped.

Hailey found the book on the shelf behind Grandma's chair, between the cookbooks. It argued that keeping a connection to someone who had died, through memories, objects, or traditions, could be a healthy part of grieving. She read the sentence three times. The word "healthy" sat there on the page, plain as a kitchen timer. Nobody in the book said anything about moving on. She checked the index for "moving on" and it was not even listed, which made her laugh once, quietly, in the empty chair room.

On the last night in the house, Hailey invited Ally and Chance over, and the three of them made oatmeal cookies using the wooden spoon, following the recipe card in Grandma's handwriting. Ally creamed the butter while Chance read the steps out loud. Hailey stirred, and she thought about how Grandma had driven her to the clinic every autumn for her flu vaccine, and had always bought her a juice box after, and how none of that was trivial. She put one warm cookie on the windowsill, which Grandma used to do for the mail carrier. "That one's hers," Hailey said, and took the apron off the hook to wear tomorrow.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.
story:
The puppy had been his for exactly four hours, and Nicholas had already named him Biscuit, mostly because of the pale patch on his back that had a kind of lopsided symmetry to it, like a cookie someone had bitten on one side. Biscuit was small enough to fit in a shoebox, curious about everything, and especially interested in Nicholas's backpack, which was lying open on the kitchen floor. "No, that's homework," Nicholas said, gently pulling the bag away. Biscuit sneezed, wobbled over to the water bowl, and then, while Nicholas wasn't looking, went back for a second try. Nicholas only noticed when he heard the crinkle of a foil wrapper.

He counted the gum pieces left in the pack. There had been eight, the sugar-free kind his mom bought, and now there were five. His stomach dropped. He had seen a poster at the animal shelter that morning, the one beside the cage where Biscuit had been sleeping in a curled-up ball like a nocturnal creature pretending the fluorescent lights weren't real. The poster had listed foods that were dangerous for dogs, and one line had jumped out at him: xylitol. He remembered turning the word over in his head, wondering what it even was. Now he dug the empty wrappers out from under the couch and found the word printed right there on the foil. His mom's sugar-free gum.

"Mom!" he shouted. "Biscuit ate three pieces of gum. The kind with xylitol in it." He was already scooping up the puppy, whose dark eyes refract... whose eyes caught the kitchen light and threw it back at him in two tiny bright points, as if Biscuit had no idea anything was wrong. "That's bad for dogs," his mom said, grabbing her keys. "I read that it makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar. It's not like it is for us. Call the vet, tell them we're coming."

At the clinic, Ms. Sadeghi, who turned out to be the veterinarian and also, impossibly, the mother of Nikola from his science class, took Biscuit behind the counter immediately. Nicholas stood at the window watching the sun refract through the fish tank in the waiting room, a small rainbow trembling on the wall, and tried not to imagine the worst. Through the door he heard her say, "We'll get his blood sugar up and watch him for a while. You caught it fast, and that matters." An hour later Biscuit came out wagging his whole back end, shameless, and Nikola appeared beside Nicholas with two juice boxes. "So my mom says your dog ate gum," Nikola said. Nicholas looked down at Biscuit, who was already sniffing Nikola's pocket. "Check your pockets," Nicholas said. "Check them right now."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Closing a switch completes the circuit so current flows; opening it makes a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once.
story:
The sign at the science museum said MAKE IT LIGHT UP, and Jayden grabbed the little model house before Khaleesi could. "I call dibs on the wiring," he said. "I've done this at school."

Khaleesi raised an eyebrow. "You shorted out a buzzer with a paperclip."

"That was a design choice."

Mr. Littlechild, the volunteer in the blue vest, set out the parts: a battery, a switch, a bulb, and a pile of wire. "The house has to light up when you flip the switch," he said. "That's the whole challenge."

Jayden snapped the wires into place, taped the battery in, and flipped the switch. Nothing. He flipped it again, faster, as if the bulb were just slow. Still nothing.

"Maybe the bulb's dead," Khaleesi said.

Jayden unscrewed the bulb and touched it straight to the battery. It glowed instantly. So the bulb was fine, which meant the problem was hiding somewhere he couldn't see. He stared at the loop of wire. The current had to travel all the way around, through the battery, the switch, and the bulb, or nothing happened. One gap anywhere stopped everything. Somewhere in that loop was a hole.

He'd been naive to trust the tape job, he decided. He walked the loop with one finger, wire by wire, and found it: a clip at the switch had slipped loose. He pushed it back until it clicked.

"Flip it," he said, and closed his eyes.

The bulb blazed. Khaleesi whooped so loudly that a toddler across the room pointed at their house in wonder.

"Okay," Khaleesi admitted, "you may keep your dibs. But when the bulb burns out, I'm rewiring it."

"You'd have to resign from Team Dibs first."

Jayden flipped the switch off, watched the light vanish, and flipped it on again just to feel the whole loop obey him at once. "See?" he said. "One gap, one finger, one click."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
story:
Blake sat at the kitchen table with a blank sheet of paper, a pencil, and two very different ideas about strawberries. Mr. Das had assigned each student one question: why do strawberries cost less in summer than in winter? Blake was supposed to explain it with a diagram.

He drew two lines that crossed like an X and labeled one "supply" and the other "demand." It looked right, but he could not say why. He stared at the crossing point and wondered who had first thought of drawing it that way. It seemed like a strange thing to invent, two lines fighting over a dot.

His phone buzzed. Valerie had sent a photo of her own diagram, which was, annoyingly, neater. "Yours looks like a broken kite," she texted. He called her.

"I have to confess something," he said. "I traced mine off a cereal box."

"That's not even a real thing."

"It could be." He put her on speaker and typed into the search bar: who made the supply and demand diagram famous. He read out loud as the page loaded. "Alfred Marshall. A British economist. He popularized it, the two crossing curves, in his 1890 book." He scrolled. "It's called Principles of Economics."

"Nineteen hundred years ago?" Valerie said.

"Eighteen ninety. That's still ancient. That's before television."

Blake looked back at his kite-shaped X and suddenly understood his own drawing. More strawberries in summer meant his supply line slid sideways, and the crossing point dropped to a lower price. Fewer in winter, and it climbed back up. He redrew the lines twice, once for each season, and wrote "cheap here" and "expensive here" in tiny letters.

"What if the whole thing is about empathy?" Valerie said. "Like, the farmer feels bad charging five dollars in January?"

"No, the farmer feels fine. The farmer has almost no strawberries."

Blake carried the paper to the fridge and pinned it under the strawberry-shaped magnet, which was, he now noticed, holding up a grocery list that included strawberries.

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: A soliloquy is a speech a character gives alone on stage, letting the audience hear the character's private thoughts.
story:
Kaitlyn stood alone at the center of the empty auditorium stage, script rolled tight in her fist. Mr. Hu had cast her as the girl who talks to the empty kitchen at midnight, and for three days she had been stuck. "Who am I even talking to?" she called down to the third row, where Leandro and Meadow sat with their feet on the seat backs.

"To nobody," Leandro said. "That's the whole point. It's a soliloquy, a speech a character gives alone on stage so the audience can hear her private thoughts."

Kaitlyn unrolled the script and looked at it differently now. She had presumed the speech needed an imagined listener, a friend standing invisible in the wings, but that was why it felt fake. The character wasn't performing for anyone. She was thinking out loud. She tried the first line again, slower, letting the words arrive like real thoughts instead of launched arrows. When she hit the line about the broken locket, she stopped, looked at her own hand, and let the pause stretch until Meadow leaned forward.

"That pause," Meadow said. "Do that one again."

They ran it six times. Kaitlyn experimented with a hypothetical question she raised for herself: what if she did the whole speech sitting on the stage edge, as if the character had given up standing? The fourth try was clumsy and the fifth was worse, but on the sixth something clicked, and Leandro whistled.

By Friday, word had spread that Kaitlyn's monologue was worth watching, and her reputation pulled a few stray sixth graders into the seats at lunch. Mr. Hu watched from the back, arms crossed, saying nothing until the end. Then he climbed the steps, nodded once, and said, "Opening night, you do it exactly like that."

Kaitlyn grinned and rolled her script even tighter, like a microphone.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
At Hadassah's kitchen table, Lily typed her old blog's name into Hadassah's phone, chewing her thumbnail. Two years ago, in third grade, she had written a blog about her hamster, Biscuit, and she had deleted it last spring when she got embarrassed. Now Parker kept saying he'd found something, and she wanted to see for herself. "It's gone," she said. "I deleted it. I watched it disappear."

"Try this," Parker said, leaning over her shoulder. He typed the name of a website she'd never heard of, then pasted her blog's address into a search box. "My cousin showed me. It's called the Wayback Machine."

The page loaded, and Lily's stomach dropped. There was her blog, exactly as it had looked in third grade, pink background, wobbly hamster drawings and all. Below the address, a whole row of dates. "Since 1996," Hadassah read from a little note on the screen, "the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages." She scrolled, and snapshot after snapshot of Lily's old posts slid past. "So deleting it only deleted it for you."

Lily clicked the oldest post. There was Biscuit's cage, and behind it, propped against the wall, a piece of paper she'd photographed without thinking: the school permission slip with her full address printed at the top. She had been so proud of Biscuit's new wheel that she hadn't looked at anything else in the picture. "Anybody could read this," she said quietly. "Anybody at all."

"That's why I don't post where I am," Hadassah said, dunking a biscuit in her milk. "My mum says the internet never really hibernates. It just pretends to."

Parker grinned. "You've been feeding it like a consumer feeds a vending machine, and it keeps everything." Lily stuck her tongue out at him, but she was already drafting a message to the archive's help address on Hadassah's phone:

Dear Internet Archive, I am ten years old and my old blog has my home address on a slip of paper in a photo. I deleted the blog before I knew copies were saved. Could you please take that page down? I would appreciate it very much. Sincerely, Lily.

She read it out loud, and Hadassah said it sounded very grown up, except the part where she'd written that Biscuit had gone to live on a farm, which was technically true but also the defiant lie she'd told in third grade instead of saying he'd escaped for two days.

They sent the message. Then Lily opened the camera app and turned it around, so the screen showed only the ceiling and Hadassah's laughing face. "New rule," she said. "From now on, we photograph the wheel, not the wall."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
Vincent stood in the middle of the empty living room, his voice bouncing off bare walls. The moving truck had come that morning, and tomorrow it would carry everything to the new town, six hours away. He had argued against the move for weeks, doing everything he could to oppose his parents' plan, and he had lost. Now his sneakers squeaked on the wooden floor, and the only sound in the whole house was his own footsteps.

His phone buzzed. It was Mika, calling from the porch next door, where she sat on the railing swinging her legs. "I figured out something," she said. "My cousin moved to Denver three years ago and she never calls anybody, and now she doesn't have a single friend from here. But my grandma moved away from her best friend when she was our age, and they still talk every single week. They visit each other and send messages and everything." Vincent turned in a slow circle, thinking. Friends who stayed close were friends who kept in touch, and friends who faded were the ones who let the contact stop. It was a real pattern, not just a guess. If the inference was right, then the whole thing depended on what he and Mika did next, not on the distance. "So we can't just say goodbye and hope," he said. "We have to actually plan it."

"Exactly," said Mika. "That's what I want. Sunday afternoons, video call, every week. Same time, no excuses. If one of us misses it, the other one calls twice as much until we catch up." They hammered out the details right there, Vincent shouting through the window and Mika laughing from her railing. She made him promise to show her his new room first, even if the walls were scuzzy. "If it's dilapidated, I definitely have to see it," she said.

The next morning, Vincent climbed into the car while the movers locked the truck. He looked back at the house shrinking in the mirror, then down at his phone, where he typed a message to Mika: "Sunday, three o'clock. First call. I'll show you everything." Then he pressed send.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: When asking a stranger for directions, Spanish speakers usually use the polite usted, French speakers vous, and German speakers Sie, rather than the familiar form.
story:
Alexis stood on her grandmother's porch with a box of old paperbacks under one arm. Her grandmother had agreed to drive her into town so she could donate the books to the library, but first the car had to be found, because her grandmother had lent it to a neighbour and could not remember which street the neighbour lived on. "Ask Frau Keller," her grandmother said. "Two streets over. But you will have to ask in German, because she answers to nobody in English."

Alexis had been practising German all summer, and she knew the words she needed. She walked down the hill, found an old woman watering roses, and said, "Wo wohnst du?" The woman looked at her, watered another rose, and said nothing at all. Alexis tried again, louder. The woman turned her back. On the walk back up the hill Alexis made a list in her head: the woman was not deaf, because she had flinched at a car horn. She was not unfriendly, because she had waved at a boy on a bicycle. The only variable left was the words themselves, and the one word Alexis had chosen was du.

She had an idea, and it was a small one. Back at the house she found her German notebook and looked up the polite form. Then she walked down the hill a second time and said, "Wo wohnen Sie, Frau Keller?" The woman set down the hose and smiled and pointed left, then right, then said something with drei and Häusern in it. Three houses from the corner, painted green. Alexis found the car parked outside it, and taped to the windscreen was a note with the library's address and a map.

At the library she called her friend Lacey, who was taking Spanish at summer camp. "Ask your counsellor for directions and see what happens," Alexis said. "Try the familiar form first." Lacey reported back an hour later: an older woman at the camp had ignored a casual tú until a boy switched to usted, and then the directions came out all at once, with hand gestures. "My French pen pal says it's vous over there," Lacey added. "Whether the hand gestures help or just confuse you is subjective, but the pronoun part isn't." Alexis laughed and said her dilemma was solved either way, since she now had a ride, a map, and a rule worth testing on her grandmother, who spoke only German to neighbours.

That evening Alexis said, "Oma, hast du mein Buch gesehen?" Her grandmother kept peeling potatoes. Alexis waited, then tried, "Haben Sie mein Buch gesehen?" Her grandmother looked up at once and held out the missing book from under a newspaper. Alexis took it and studied her grandmother's face. "You understood me the first time," she said. Her grandmother went back to her potatoes and said, "Sie hat gut gefragt."

story:
Brayden flopped onto the couch with his phone and opened the group chat, where Van had posted a photo of the whole soccer team outside the pizza place, jerseys on, grinning. "Wait," Brayden typed. "You put our team name AND the pizza place tag on this?" Terrance replied with three laughing emojis, then, "so? it's funny." Brayden frowned at the little map pin under the photo. "It says where we were. Like exactly where."

"You worry more than my grandma," Van sent, and the chat filled up with crying-laughing faces. Brayden set the phone down, then picked it up again, because something was itching at him. Last month Terrance had searched his own name for a school project and found a comment he'd written in third grade on a public fan page, sitting right there in the results like it had been waiting for him. Terrance had howled about it for a week. Brayden had asked his cousin why the old comment showed up, and his cousin had shrugged and said, "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. Public stuff gets found." Brayden hadn't really believed it until he'd tried it himself.

Now he typed into the chat: "experiment. everybody search your own name right now." He did the same, holding his breath, and there it was, the team photo from last season that Van had posted publicly, with a caption naming the school. Third result. Underneath it, their tournament schedule, including the field they practiced at every Tuesday.

The chat went quiet except for typing dots, then dots, then dots. Terrance broke first: "WHY AM I ON THE INTERNET." Van sent, "okay. okay okay okay. deleting." His typing technique was frantic, whole messages appearing in bursts, half of them misspelled. "Can you delete it everywhere though," Brayden wondered out loud to the empty room. Copies felt kind of inevitable once something was out there, but at least they could stop feeding it.

Van changed the chat settings so only members could see posts, then sent a new picture: his cat wearing a tiny soccer sock as a hat. "location: my couch," he wrote. "you're welcome."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
Brooklyn sat at the kitchen table with her half-built robot prototype, a little car made from a sponge soaked so porous with glue it would never roll again. She was supposed to be finishing it for the science club, but she kept checking her phone. Lily-Anne had not texted back in four days.

It had started when Brooklyn joined robotics and Lily-Anne joined track. Their schedules stopped matching, and then their conversations did too. Last week Lily-Anne had said, "You'd rather hang out with Abbas and his circuit boards," and walked away before Brooklyn could answer. Abbas was fine, but he was not Lily-Anne.

Brooklyn scraped glue off the table and thought about it like a science problem. When she and Lily-Anne had liked all the same things, the friendship had practically run itself. Now they liked different things, and it was stalling. She remembered a page Ms. Krause had printed for the class, and dug it out of her backpack. A 2015 study had followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade, and the friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end. "So that's the pattern," Brooklyn said out loud. If sameness was what kept friendships going, she could not magically become a runner. But she could find one new thing they both actually cared about.

She texted Lily-Anne: "Can you come over? I need a runner." Twenty minutes later Lily-Anne stood in the doorway, arms crossed, still in her track warmups.

"I need someone fast to test this," Brooklyn said, holding up the little car. "If it works, we enter it together in the science fair. You'd have to participate, though. Practice runs, timing, all of it."

Lily-Anne uncrossed her arms. "I get to be the one who says go?"

"You're the only one fast enough to catch it."

Lily-Anne took the car gently, like it was a baby bird, and set it on the hallway floor. "Okay," she said. "On three. One, two, go."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
The stands at the rink were so loud that Alexis could feel the noise in his teeth. He was squeezed between his dad and Casey, with Markus one row down, watching the championship game. When the home team scored the tying goal, Markus stood up and yelled like his voice alone could push the puck into the net, and Alexis found himself yelling too.

Afterward, waiting in line for hot chocolate while the teams skated warm-ups for overtime, Casey said, "If we cheer loud enough, they'll win. That's how home ice works." Alexis stirred his cocoa. He remembered something Ms. Chaudhry had shown their class back in the fall, a newspaper story from her scrapbook of odd sports facts. In the 2020 NFL season, she'd told them, when almost no fans were allowed in the stadiums because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. Basically, no home advantage at all. Alexis had rolled his eyes at the time and copied it down only because it might be on a quiz. Now he turned it over in his head. If cheering really made teams win, then a whole season of empty stadiums should have turned out lopsided, road teams losing left and right. It hadn't. It had come out almost perfectly even.

"I don't think the noise does it," Alexis said slowly. "There was that football season with no fans, and home teams went 127-128-1." Casey squinted at him. "So when I scream at the TV, it does nothing?" Alexis shrugged. "Maybe it does something. Just not that." Ms. Chaudhry, in line behind them buying coffee for the zamboni driver she knew, laughed. "Careful," she said. "Half the commerce in this building depends on people believing yelling helps. Pucks, foam fingers, that sign shop that will modify any jersey with your name by the third period."

Overtime started. The crowd rose, and a banner reading HOME OF THE CONTEMPORARY CHAMPIONS unrolled over the rail. Markus was already on his feet again, banging the boards with both fists. Alexis stood up beside him. He still didn't know if it mattered, and he wasn't sure he wanted to know. When the puck dropped, he cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted anyway.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: At a council meeting, a proposal usually needs one member to move it and another to second it before council debates and votes on it.
story:
The bench outside the skate park had been removed in May, and Alex wanted it back. His grandfather's house was the quietest place he knew, with the smell of old books and toast, so that was where he spread out his petition papers on the kitchen table. Grandpa sliced apples beside him but said nothing except, "Councillor Rao has her office hours on Thursdays." Alex had gathered forty signatures at school, including Quinton's enormous scrawl and Axelle's tidy loops, and he had written a speech. What he did not have was any idea what happened after he handed the papers over.

On Thursday, Councillor Rao read every signature. "This is good work," she said. "I can bring your bench to a council meeting as a motion. But I can't just stand up and talk. A proposal needs one member to move it and another to second it before council debates and votes on it." She tapped the petition. "Without a seconder, it dies right there." Alex asked if she had a seconder, and she smiled in a way that did not answer him, which worried him for three straight days.

Grandpa drove him to the council meeting on Tuesday night. The chamber smelled like floor polish and coffee, and the chairs were the hard parallel rows of a courtroom, all facing the long curved desk where seven councillors sat. Alex clutched his notes. When his item came up, Councillor Rao stood, said she was moving a motion to restore the bench at Harlow Park, and mentioned the forty names on the petition as testimony from the neighbourhood. Then she sat down, and the room went still.

Alex gripped the edge of his seat. Nobody moved. The chair at the end was empty, its microphone dark, and it dawned on him that one of the seven councillors was missing tonight. If that was the person who would have seconded it, then the whole thing, signatures, speech, apples and worry, was finished. A door at the side creaked. A woman in a raincoat hurried in, whispered something to the clerk, and slid into the empty chair.

"I'll second that," the woman said, still catching her breath. She nodded at Councillor Rao, then turned slightly, as if she knew exactly where Alex was sitting. Later, outside, Grandpa found him still holding his unused notes. "You didn't even get to speak," Grandpa said.

"I didn't need to," Alex said, and he watched the rain begin to dot the pavement, each drop making its own small dark circle.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
Connor spread his notebook across the kitchen table and stared at the two numbers he had written there. His rubber-band launcher had thrown a marshmallow 240 centimeters on the first try and only 90 on the second. Tomorrow he was supposed to tell Khalid the average range, and right now the average was meaningless, because the two trials couldn't even agree on a neighborhood.

"You look like your project bit you," said Khalid, dropping into the other chair and reaching for a marshmallow. Khalid wanted to eat the ammunition, which was a problem, because every marshmallow he ate was one fewer launch. "Just write down the big number," he said. "Two hundred forty sounds amazing on a poster."

Connor thought about last year's fair, when he had claimed his paper airplane flew eight meters off one single throw that had caught a lucky gust. Mr. Lawson had asked him to repeat it, and it had gone two meters, and Connor had stood there with his face burning. He wasn't going to be that narrator of his own disaster twice. "No," he said. "One throw can be a fluke either way. I'm going to run it ten times and average all ten."

"Ten? That's so many."

"You'll comply with the rules of science," Connor said, loading the launcher. "Or at least with mine."

They took turns launching while Connor's mom timed nothing and understood nothing but kept the cocoa coming. Trial three went 110. Trial four went 230, and Khalid insisted the wind from the open window had helped, so Connor closed it and marked the number anyway. By trial ten they had a messy column of numbers from 85 to 250, and when Connor added them up and divided, the average came out 148.

"One forty-eight," Khalid said, chewing a marshmallow he had stolen from trial seven. "That's not amazing."

"It's true," Connor said, and wrote it in big assertive letters at the top of the page. Then he set the launcher down in front of Khalid. "Your turn to record. We're doing all ten again."
